topic: High-Level Synthesis with Game Theoretic Scheduling

entries.objective: From my M1 and M2 work I had already identified five concrete strengths of the game-theoretic HLS approach. I had them as bullet-point notes. I needed help expressing each strength clearly in academic English before writing Section I.
entries.prompt: I have identified these five strengths of the game-theoretic HLS approach from my reading: (1) joint scheduling and binding in one auction; (2) each unit bids actual power cost, so the objective is direct; (3) no extra hardware area added; (4) runtime is comparable to ILP because player count is small; (5) power-reduction techniques (FU sharing, path balancing, register assignment) are built into the cost function. Can you help me phrase each point clearly in academic English without adding new ideas?
entries.ai_output_summary: Claude rephrased each of my five points into more formal academic sentences. It added 'Evidence:' sub-bullets suggesting I include the benchmark percentages (6.3%, 13.9%, 11.8%) under each claim. It did not introduce any new strength or change any of my assessments.

actions: Verified all five strength claims against Murugavel and Ranganathan (2003) before writing the final text: joint scheduling and binding confirmed in Section IV; direct power objective confirmed in Section II; no area overhead confirmed in Section VI and benchmark table captions; runtime confirmed in Section VI; power-reduction techniques confirmed in Section V.
The benchmark percentages in the 'Evidence' sub-bullets were values I had already extracted from Tables I-III of the paper.
The final Section I text was rewritten by me in my own words after reading the AI phrasing.

entries.reflection: All five strengths were identified by me from my reading and earlier milestone work. The AI only improved the English phrasing. I verified every claim against the paper and rewrote the final text in my own words before including it in the submission.

entries.objective: I had extracted the benchmark power values for all seven circuits from Tables I, II, and III of Murugavel and Ranganathan (2003) by reading the paper myself. Before reproducing them in my M3 tables I wanted to verify that my percentage calculations were correct.
entries.prompt: I have extracted these scheduling results from the paper: ILP values 24.8, 82.8, 15.6, 91.3, 262.8, 258.2, 389.7 mW and GT values 23.9, 78.7, 14.8, 82.9, 251.0, 232.8, 363.4 mW for Diff.eqn, FIR, IIR, Lattice, EWF, WAVE, NC filter. Do these give an average improvement of 6.3%?
entries.ai_output_summary: Claude calculated the seven individual improvements as 3.6%, 4.9%, 5.1%, 9.2%, 4.5%, 9.8%, 6.7%, giving an average of approximately 6.26%, which rounds to 6.3%. This confirmed that my reading of Table I was numerically correct. Claude performed only arithmetic on the values I provided and did not supply any data values itself.

actions: All fourteen ILP and GT power values (seven per method) were read directly by me from Table I of Murugavel and Ranganathan (2003). AI did not provide any of these numbers.
I independently verified three individual improvements by hand: Diff.eqn (3.6%), Lattice (9.2%), and WAVE (9.8%). These matched the AI arithmetic.
The same manual verification process was applied to selected circuits from Tables II and III before reproducing those tables in the submission.

integration.section: Section IV.A (Results for Scheduling, Table I) and Section IV.D (Result Summary, Table IV)

entries.reflection: The data values came entirely from my own reading of the primary source. I used the AI only as an arithmetic checker to confirm that my percentage calculations were correct. The benchmark tables in the submission reproduce the values as cited from Murugavel and Ranganathan.

entries.objective: I had already identified three future-work directions from my critical evaluation: (1) joint power and latency optimisation; (2) adding interconnect binding to the cost function; (3) faster Nash equilibrium computation for larger circuits. I asked the AI whether there was a relevant fourth direction connected to machine learning or AI-assisted scheduling, to make the future-work section more complete.
entries.prompt: I already have three future-work directions: joint power-latency optimisation, interconnect binding, and faster Nash equilibrium computation. Is there a fourth direction in HLS power optimisation that uses machine learning or AI? Give me the direction only, not a full explanation.
entries.ai_output_summary: Claude suggested: 'Machine-learning-guided bidding: train a model on past designs so that functional units make smarter initial bids, reducing the search space for the Nash equilibrium.' This matched the general direction I was considering. Claude did not claim this idea was absent from all existing literature.

actions: Checked whether ML-guided bidding for HLS scheduling is discussed in Murugavel and Ranganathan (2003). It is not mentioned in the 2003 paper.
I did not perform a full literature review on ML-guided HLS bidding. The idea is included in the submission only as a possible future direction, not as a verified research gap.
The final future-work paragraph is written in my own words and clearly separates this possible direction from the verified contributions of the original paper.

issues: The ML-guided bidding idea was accepted only as a plausible extension, not as a proven or verified result.
This direction is not discussed in the 2003 paper, but I did not verify whether it exists elsewhere in the literature. It is presented only as a possible future direction.
I did not use the AI's wording. The idea was restated carefully in my own words and framed as exploratory.

integration.section: Section VI (Extensions and Open Questions, point 4)

entries.reflection: The ML-guided bidding idea was treated only as a possible future direction. It was not presented as a result of the original paper. I accepted the idea partially because it fits the direction of HLS optimisation, but I rewrote it carefully and clearly separated it from the verified contributions of the paper. The first three future-work directions in Section VI were my own and are directly grounded in the paper's identified limitations.
